utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. You are still under solemn declaration and the Prosecution will continue examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the record, I would like to advise the Bench that on Friday afternoon I did have contact with this witness just to approach her and explain that the previous witness was taking longer than anticipated, that she would not take the stand on Friday afternoon and that we would recommence with her testimony on Monday morning. So we didn't, of course, broach any topic relating to her testimony, it was just to advise the witness of that and to welcome her back to The Hague. But I would like the Bench to know that that contact did take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Very well

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Welcome back, Ms. Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you were here in the Tribunal, you had testified about your life in Bosanski Samac in April and May 1992, and you had testified to the Chamber about a period of time you spent in detention in Crkvina, starting on -- in and around the 15th of May, 1992. Do you recall giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When we broke with your testimony, you had explained to the Chamber how you had been taken away from Crkvina in a truck, you had been brought back to your house on Edvarda Kardelja Street, and you had been deposited there. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, I'd like to ask you questions now from that time period on, from the time that you arrived back in your apartment on Edvarda Kardelja Street. When you arrived back at your apartment, was your then boyfriend waiting for you at the apartment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What was the first thing you did when you returned to your apartment, having been in detention?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we improvised a bath, because I was fairly dirty, and I hoped that I'd be able to relax in my own -- once back in my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were you able to relax?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regrettably, no. This joy lasted only two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What happened after approximately two hours after you had arrived back in your flat?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment arrived, headed by Cakara. They banged on the door. Normally, my husband let them in, and again they repeated the procedure which existed before, looking and hunting for automatic weapons from me, asking them from me and my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned one person called Cakara. This is a nickname, is it?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's a nickname. Cakara is from Samac, and throughout that time, I was always mixing him up, Cakara and Caba, but Cakara's name is Naser. So Naser came, but he has the nickname Cakara. He was leading that group that entered my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I understand you said they looked -- you said they were looking for weapons. Did they find any weapons?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they searched the entire apartment. They were very rough, in view of the fact that in the apartment they found nothing. After that, they said they would be looking by the floors. They already checked all the apartments. They still had the attic to search.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did they then conduct a search on the attic?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This operation lasted quite some time. They removed the insulation from the attic area, and when they didn't succeed in finding anything, they set afire the attic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to intervene. I heard, as all -- I heard the witness say that all the apartments were already searched [In English] already checked all the apartments. [Interpretation] I would -- did they check all the apartments? Did they search all the apartments or that all the apartments had already been searched? What did the witness say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, clear that, please, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, I don't know if you followed that intervention. Defence counsel would like some clarification as to what exactly the members of the 4th Detachment, the men who came to your house, did in respect of the other apartments. Did they search all the other apartments or had the other apartments already all been searched, or what exactly did they do?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exclusively located in my apartment. They were searching exclusively my apartment. And as they didn't find anything there, they went up to the last upper floor, where the attic was, and that is what they searched. I was interested why only us, and they told us that the other apartments had been searched. But what did they comprehend and intend by that, that all the apartments were clean, I don't know, but the question -- the open issue was my apartment, and I don't know what they were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So the men who searched your apartment told you that the other apartments had previously been searched; is that correct, but they didn't carry out a search in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. They searched in front of me only my apartment, completely, and that attic area in our entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they find anything in the attic area?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They didn't have anything to be -- there was nothing to be found, and they didn't find it. We simply didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did anything else happen in the attic at this time when they were searching the attic?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can imagine the tension. I personally was afraid that maybe somebody planted some weapons. In my previous statement, I mentioned that my former boyfriend, present-day husband, was fit for military service, and maybe they would plant it and in connection with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was the attic set fire to that day?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this entire ceremony, the aggressive action, and out of their bad mood, they set the cellar -- the attic afire with insulation which ignites very quickly. Then I didn't do anything there. I was just looking. And my husband attempted to put out the fire as quickly as possible. So this is a building with 64 apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Kapetanovic, just for the record, the transcript in English has a record of you saying that they set the cellar and then you changed it to the attic on fire. If I'm correct, you didn't mention the cellar. It's only the attic that was set on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been speaking throughout about the attic area.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After the attic was set on fire, did these members of the 4th Detachment leave your apartment building?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They left the apartment building and also added that they would be coming back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you remain in your apartment building after this search?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the very same moment, my boyfriend at the time collected me and my dog and took me to the -- to a cellar in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And this cellar, was it a private cellar belonging to someone's house?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was a private house.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And do I take it, then, you were taken there as a form of safety, a safety measure, or for better protection for yourself?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My husband acted very quickly, spontaneously. I don't know how he remembered to take me to a very specific house and into that cellar of that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that cellar?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, quite a long time. So it was the end of May, and I returned to my apartment somewhere in July. I don't know -- I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: For some time, then, just over a month, was it?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you remember the family who owned this -- the name of the family who owned this house where you took shelter?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The owner of the house, she was not present, but her son and daughter were there. It was a family home of the family Bikic, mother -- I don't remember the mother's name. The daughter's name was Ismeta, and the son was Adem Bikic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was one of the families -- was one of the members of the family a person called Dino Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the son of Ismeta Halilovic, and I must add that the Halilovic family lived in the same building as I did. And they called it Dedo's family, Dedo the person, the man, was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say they lived in the same building as you did, you're now talking about 62 Edvarda Kardelja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your husband, Esref Kapetanovic, and this person Dino Halilovic have to perform forced labour?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two of them grew up together. They worked together in the post office. And when they had to go and do forced labour, they went there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they have any choice in whether or not they went to perform this force the labour?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. Who would want to go and do this type of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What type of forced labour were they performing?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of them concretely worked in the Master company. That is auto transporters. And in that company, my husband was working on the maintenance, the repair of the vehicles, the cleaning of that company premises, and all other difficult, heavy work, and it covered trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your husband have to perform this duty every day?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in case the need arose, if the request was made, he went and repaired telecommunications in the neighbouring villages, and that was rather dangerous, because they were taken to the front lines to repair the communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your husband ever taken to locations where he was exposed to firing from weapons?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen that in order to repair a telecommunication line, my husband would have to climb a pole, a pole of five, six metres, or even more, and you can imagine what it was like. In the area of Grebnice or Obudovac, a highly critical point, bullets were whistling over their heads or past them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your husband ever receive any payment for the work that he was required to do?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was a parody and that they laughed, yes. My husband was paid by saying that the salary which he received after one month, I could receive two eggs. So it was symbolic, or a parody.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you -- was your husband given cash into his hand or was he told he would get money, or how was this parody of a payment, as you called it, made?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was into his hand, without any document. He received the salary in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you -- if you recall at this moment, could you tell us roughly how much that was?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, no, but I know that for that amount, we bought two eggs. The inflation was very high. The dinar was in use, which was then changed into Serbian dinars, but the value -- or -- the value I did get to know quite well, the worth of this money.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So do I understand correctly: Was it that from all the money that he received for all the forced labour that he performed during his time in Bosanski Samac, you were able to purchase two eggs for that amount.

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. For the entire amount, the entire amount that my husband received for his work, from morning to night, at the end we did buy in fact two eggs. Nothing else could be bought. That was the amount.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. During this month in the cellar of a neighbourhood house, how did you survive for food and water?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The electricity and water didn't -- were not supplied, but in the neighbouring street, women had -- a woman had a pump and we took cannisters. Eight of us lived in that house, together with my dog. We came to that house from three other houses, so that the boys who could enter the buildings, they went to our homes, our apartments. They would take out what we had left there. So these were noodles, then meat, and as there was no electricity, some food perished. Therefore, we lived on noodles.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've testified that you did go back to your own apartment. What caused you to leave this cellar and return to your own apartment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, namely, my husband told me, that the family who lived in my entrance, that they are showing an interest in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by the fact that one of the families in your apartment block were showing an interest in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The woman - her name is Vera Avdic, and she had -- her husband was a Muslim but was a member of the 4th Detachment. He had the right for benefits, namely, they had an apartment and they had a young girl with a boyfriend who was dating a member of the 4th Detachment. And they -- I assume they expected, as a reward from the 4th Detachment, that they would be receiving my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you moved back to your apartment block, were you then allowed to live there in peace?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a certain period of time, yes. I was lucky. And my neighbour, Luka Culumovic, maintained all my belongings. He took care of my apartment. I returned home to an area which was not looted, and regrettably, I stayed there for a relatively short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Ms. Kapetanovic, I believe you testified you moved back to your apartment sometime in July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there up to the time after my husband fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And do you remember the date or the approximate date of when your husband fled?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An important call-up of the non-Serbs was underway, namely, it referred to the remaining Croats and the Muslims. In view of the fact that my husband didn't want to take up arms and go and fight, he decided, together with his friends, to flee across the River Sava to Croatia. That was on the 22nd or the 23rd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you leave your apartment then immediately after your husband fled towards the end of August, or were you removed from your apartment for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed and lived in that apartment, together with the dog. It was difficult. It was an extremely difficult time. And a woman -- for a woman to live alone. I don't think it's necessary to emphasise this. The nights were really problematic. I didn't leave on my own there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Why did you leave your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since some 120 non-Serbs escaped from Samac, a large-scale arrest of Muslim families ensued and, to a lesser degree, Croat families, because most of them had already been arrested. They went door to door, from family to family, and took away entire families towards Zasavica. Something similar happened to me as well, although I, being a girlfriend of somebody who had escaped, believed that I would be spared this arrest because my husband, my boyfriend, had a family. I was sad about that. His father is a handicapped person and had been in the wheelchair for 24 years, so I personally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, would you control the flow of evidence? Can we deal with facts, please, events, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Kapetanovic, I need you will to be more specific in your answers to my questions and more brief in your responses. Were you arrested and taken to Zasavica after your boyfriend escaped across the river?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I want to ask a few questions about your time between your return to the apartment and this second arrest and removal to Zasavica. Whilst you were still living in your apartment, did you make any approaches to the defendant Miroslav Tadic about leaving Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did contact him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And where did you go to contact Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the office of Mr. Tadic, which was in the local commune building at the time. So I went directly to him, to his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were you able to see Mr. Tadic immediately or did you have to wait a while before you saw him?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see him immediately because there were other people, soldiers, members of the 4th Detachment, waiting before me, so I sat in the hallway and waited there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were waiting in the hallway, did you overhear any of the business that Mr. Tadic was conducting, specifically with members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I naturally did. I sat right next to the door, which was open towards the hallway. I heard the conversation between representatives of those soldiers and Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And what was the topic of those conversations you overheard?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topic was a very sad one. It had to do with those who were killed during combat. They were supposed to bury them and they asked him what could they offer in terms of assistance to the families of the fallen soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it your impression from what you heard that it was Miroslav Tadic who would decide what would be distributed to families of the fallen soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. He was the one who decided what was to be given to those families. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you eventually get to speak with Mr. Tadic yourself?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to reach him and talk to Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And what did you ask Mr. Tadic when you got to meet him?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him to put me on the list for exchanges, which were ongoing at the time, so that I could leave Samac and finally reunite with my family. I offered him my apartment in return for this exchange, and also my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic accept your offer of the apartment and your house?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. He told me that I could expect everyone from Samac leave, but that I wouldn't be able to leave so easily and that I knew very well why was that so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What was your interpretation of what Mr. Tadic meant when he said that you knew very well why you would not be leaving?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, it's not speculation?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness her interpretation of a statement that was made to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a proper question, so you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Kapetanovic, can you explain what your interpretation was in that office when Mr. Tadic told you that you knew very well why you would not be leaving?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I naturally knew why he told this to me. Mr. Tadic knows that I'm from Croatia. He knows that my entire family belonged to the HVO. He also knew that my boyfriend had escaped and joined the same forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This meeting with Mr. Tadic, it took place, then, after the end of August, when your boyfriend had escaped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it your understanding, then, from that meeting that Mr. Tadic would decide who would leave Bosanski Samac and who wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. My exchange was out of question.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And if you wanted to leave Bosanski Samac voluntarily, would you have been allowed to do so? I mean, you said you wanted to leave. Could you have just walked out or did you have to partake in one of these exchanges to leave?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was ever able to leave Bosanski Samac voluntarily. The only path to freedom was through exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Kapetanovic, could you very briefly just explain to the Chamber why, although you had stayed in Bosanski Samac through April, May, June, that you finally decided you wanted to leave Bosanski Samac? Was it voluntarily of your own will that you wanted to leave Bosanski Samac or were there circumstances that made you feel you had no choice but to leave?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple to explain that. Can you imagine living in a closed-up space, without electricity, water, money, food, without anybody around you, in a situation where they banged on your door during the night to perhaps rape you; in daytime you would sit there and wait for them to check your apartment. One lived in his or her apartment as if in prison. So who could endure such a life? Since there were no communication lines, I had no contact with my family. There was shelling going on. The war was going on, gentlemen. So to live in a closed-up space, without any basic necessities, without food, was equal to suicide. So I simply desired to leave this town that was in fact a camp, regardless of the fact that I had to leave all I had in order to escape. I simply wanted to continue living.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us whether or not the circumstances you described are the same for the non-Serbs living in your apartment? You mentioned one family, the Abdics. Did they endure this banging on the doors and the fear, et cetera, which you've just testified to?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't have to go through that. Since it was a family whose one member belonged to the 4th Detachment, so they had regular supplies of food. He had a salary. His wife had contacts with her family and freedom of movement. We were not in the same situation. We did not have same rights. These people led a normal life. They lived freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now ask you about your arrest that you've testified to. This took place in -- or did this take place in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Prior to the arrest, two days before I was actually arrested, members of special forces came and said they were from Bosanski Brod. They asked me a few questions pertaining to my boyfriend.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they were investigating situations where people had escaped?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. They asked me of precisely such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On this occasion, did the members of the forces who came to your apartment search your house or ill-treat you in any way?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They simply talked to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And then they left without providing you with any further information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They left, and I thought that was it, that I was free.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Two days later did other members of the special forces or the 4th Detachment or members of the police come to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happened early in the morning. They woke me up, banging on my door.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall now the date or the approximate date that this would have occurred on?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So I understand they banged on your door early in the morning. Could you then tell the Chamber, in as concise a manner as possible, what happened after you heard the banging.

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was in bed, I got up quickly. I opened the door. I saw Naser, called Cakara, at the door again. He said that he came to fetch me and take me to Zasavica. He was not alone. Either at my door or on the staircase, where I heard noise later on. He simply told me to go down, to enter the truck, to take my documents, do not fail to take my documents, and that was all that he allowed me to take.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that this man Cakara was not alone, and then the transcript says that "either at my door or on the staircase, where I heard noise later on." Do you mean that there was other soldiers accompanying this Cakara also at your door or other locations in the stairwell?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have a small objection regarding this question. She didn't actually -- the witness actually didn't say that these were soldiers. If I'm reading this transcript correctly, the question was members of special forces for the detachment or police, and she never answered that. So now it looks that counsel for the Prosecution actually putting some words in mouth of the witness that she never actually said. Maybe she should clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. I think counsel is correct in observing that. Can you clarify that with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Kapetanovic, could you tell us, to the best of your knowledge, who this person Cakara worked for? Was it the police or the 4th Detachment or was he a member of the special forces?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser, called Cakara, was a policeman before the war. I knew him very well. He was a member of the 4th Detachment and a very active member at that, because on several occasions it was him, exclusively him, who addressed me, and not others in the group. So this was a man who was very active.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was he -- Ms. Kapetanovic, was this man, Mr. Cakara, was he dressed in a police uniform or a camouflage uniform, or can you recall now?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore -- I did not see anybody wearing regular police uniforms during the time when I lived in the apartment. These were camouflage uniforms. Only the insignia differed, their emblems, military insignia. I have little knowledge of it. But he had a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I ask a question, going a bit back. When they were banging at your door and you told the Bench that you were in bed when you went to open the door. Were you fully dressed in your bed or, if not, did you get time to dress before you were taken down to the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wore my pajamas, and this is how I was dressed when I opened the door. When they started banging on the door, I was so scared that I wasn't even thinking about what I was wearing. I had to open the door immediately. So I opened the door in my pajamas. Later on they allowed me to get dressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of the conversation, they allowed me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, I understand that Cakara was not the only person who came to your apartment. Is that correct? He was not alone?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I saw several men dressed in the same way, but he personally addressed me, not the others. It was him.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the other men dressed also in camouflage uniform local Serbs, to the best of your knowledge, or were they Serbs from Serbia or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This second arrest was carried out by locals. I don't know their names, but I knew their faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were sent downstairs and you had taken your personal documents with you. Did you take any other personal items, clothing, personal toiletries, any personal belongings with you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had my dog in my arms at the time, my dog called Pegi, and my personal documents, or rather, my identification card, and the dog. That's all I had in my arms as I was going down to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your neighbour, Luka Culumovic, manage to give you some of your personal clothes to take with you?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to this arrest, I had two bags prepared, because I was hoping that I would be able to go through a normal exchange with the assistance of Mr. Tadic. But since this arrest was unexpected, I was only able to carry my dog, because my main concern was to have Pegi come with me to the exchange. The bags were not important.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Culumovic take one of these bags you prepared and give it to you when you were downstairs, outside your apartment block?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the truck there was a commotion, a problem. I was allowed to enter the truck, but not my dog. I begged them, and I told them that I would not get on the truck alive without my dog, because that was the only thing that I still had in my life. Then Luka came along with a bag, and now we had a double problem, because I had both the dog and the bag. And in that commotion, they said that they needed me alive, without my knowing it, Luka threw the bag into the truck and I simply carried my dog on the truck, because I didn't really care whether they killed me or they released me. It was that kind of moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This truck which was outside your apartment, was it a military truck?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To my regret, it was the same truck that had come to fetch me when they took me to Crkvina, meaning during my first arrest. It was the same truck with just two benches on each side.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it a truck with tarpaulin over the back?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was covered with tarpaulin. But the last side on the tarpaulin was opened up when I entered the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the other people on the truck when you got into the truck?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were other people there. There was Mirsada Ceribasic, a Muslim from Samac; there was Hana Bicic, or perhaps that's not her last name. I can't remember it right now. Both of these women were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And they were the only two already on the truck when you got on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was just the two of them then.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After you got on the truck, did the truck -- were any other people added to the truck at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just like during my first arrest, the truck followed the same road. We went to the neighbouring street, to the house of the woman who had been arrested with me the first time. I'm right now trying to remember her name and that of her son. She was a Catholic, a teacher, from Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: She was of Croatian ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is the woman Ruza Matic you testified to before?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for helping me remember the name. That's right. It was Mrs. Ruza Matic, and her son. We had the same misfortune to be arrested together on the first occasion and now we were arrested for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the four women on that truck -- I understand you were two Muslims and two Croats. Were you taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The truck headed towards Zasavica, and the first stop was the first checkpoint at the entrance into Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you removed from the truck at this checkpoint or was anything taken from you at this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this checkpoint, this is where I saw the special police for the first time. So the policemen checked the truck, and we had to leave the truck and our documents were not taken away from us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said that this was where you saw the special police for the first time. How did the special police differ from the people who had arrested you and the people you had seen before in Samac?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people at that checkpoint, I knew him. These were Nenad Lukic; his relative, also going by the surname of Lukic; then another person, Nenad Popovic from Obudovac; after that, they boasted that they had been promoted into the ranks of special police and they wore the police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So it was them who advised you that they were members of this special police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were people from the 4th Detachment who were promoted into special police units, and this is what Nenad told me when we talked later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you had to leave the truck, where were you taken to next?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us by truck to the house of a man named Pandurevic, surname Pandurevic. I believe that was his surname. I'll recall later. And here a mass of people from Zasavica were already waiting there. They were already arrested. And the police, who set up a police checkpoint or a reception committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kapetanovic. This man Pandurevic, was he also there at his house?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A Croat, a person of Croat ethnicity, and in his yard the people who were newly arrested were brought into his yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So the people gathered in the yard of his house, were they people from Zasavica or were they people who had been arrested in the surrounding areas and brought to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a mixed group, but a majority of these people were newly arrested. Very few people from Zasavica were still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: These mass of people who had been arrested, can you tell me what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people of Muslim ethnicity, of Croat ethnicity, as well as Croat inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you tell me if there was -- obviously yourself, women. Were there a mixture of women, children, elderly, all sorts of people who had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Entire families were collected from their homes and brought in. I didn't see anybody fit for military service. Such people already fled or they were detained in a normal prison. I'm referring here to the school or the TO or the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were all gathered here in this yard, what happened to you? Were you addressed by some of these police that you also told us were there?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told at that time that we should hand in everything we have on us, documents, money, valuables, all that we had. I gave my ID card, my pass. I succeeded in hiding my passport, and I handed in my handbag, which was -- my bag was checked, and I had no valuables. They gave me everything back except for the ID card.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was that the last time that you saw your ID card, when it was taken from you in front of Mr. Pandurevic's house?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was the last time that I saw the ID card.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: As well as taking your documents from you, did they provide you with any explanation as to why you had been arrested or what would happen to you in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just took that, my ID, they saw I had no valuables, returned my bag, and told me I was free.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When they said free, did they mean free to leave Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know at the time neither where I am, what I should do, and to whom I should turn. It was the first time that I entered that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you eventually taken to somewhere in the village where you would stay and sleep and as such make your place while you were in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inhabitant, one of the inhabitants, a lady, offered to find a place for me where I could stay. She took me along this road and tried to find out where there would be a free bed for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you eventually find some sort of accommodation in one of the houses in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end they brought me to the house of Ante Zecevic, where I already found people, but not the owner of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was Mirsada Ceribasic, who had been arrested with you, was she also taken there?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was also brought into the same house.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. The people who were there already, were they people -- you said they were not the owners. Were they people from Zasavica or people who had been detained and transferred to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people I already found there were Marko Filipovic, from Bosanski Samac; prior to that, he had been detained in the secondary school and brought in to Zasavica. That was the first person. The second person, Franjo, called Lane, known as Janje. I cannot remember the surname at this time. Yes, I do remember. Franjo Milicevic. Franjo Milicevic. And a person was there also who was also known as Toljaga. I cannot remember his name. The three of them were brought in from the secondary school and they had certain tasks to perform.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You say that these three men had certain tasks to perform. Would they be taken away during the day, required to do certain tasks, and then be brought back to the house? Is that what would happen?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The home of Ante Zecevic had a big poultry farm which the Serbs, during the war, transformed into a pig farm. And it was there that they would bring in the looted pigs, and these three persons had the duty of feeding the pigs and also of slaughtering the pigs whenever they were ordered, told, to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So these three men informed you that they had been transferred from the secondary school to Zasavica in order to take care of the pigs that the Serbs were bringing into Zasavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely so. That is right. They had to work here. That was their work duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have to do work duty while you were detained in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one morning, a person came with a list of names, where my name was also written. He said to follow him and that every morning I would have to go and work.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did this happen soon after your arrival in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you the only woman ordered to perform this duty or go to work, or were there also other female detainees who were required to work while they were detained?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the only Catholic woman who had this work duty, while all the others were Muslim women, who were from Zasavica. And I was the only Catholic woman.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said that a person came with a list of names and you had to follow him every morning. Where did you go to perform your forced labour?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a field. The truck was a part. We had to enter, board the truck. Sometimes in that truck the detainees from the secondary school were already there, and who were then taken to do the forced labour with us. And then we would be taken in the direction of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So in the mornings, would you go to the entrance of Zasavica village and meet up with everybody else who had had to do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We would walk to this field, sit -- board the truck, and then taken by truck further away.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said in the truck were detainees from the secondary school. Were these male Croats who were being detained in the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a mixed group, people of Muslim and Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So they would come in trucks from the secondary school and you would join them to go out on forced labour assignments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said that you were taken in the direction of Odzak, so I'd like to ask you questions about the forced labour in Odzak first. What types of tasks were you required to do when you were taken on these trucks to Odzak? If you could just enumerate them for the Chamber first without going into detail.

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did the following jobs: Picking plums, cleaning roads, I went looting, then corn harvest, then harvesting and picking all the fruit from the fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was the first task you were given this plum-picking?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was our first task, because at the time the plums were ripe.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you were taken to perform this plum-picking, were you accompanied by an armed guard?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always. It was compulsory.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At any stage in the time that you were picking plums did the soldiers release any rounds of fire to let you know that they were prepared to fire?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you receive any payment for this task of picking plums?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received one meal a day. We worked from the morning until dusk. And we were rewarded with one meal, if one could call that a meal, but it kept body and soul together.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Ms. Kapetanovic, I understand that you were fed once a day whilst you were taken out, but did you actually receive any payment, any money, any sort of compensation for all the work you were doing?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no money ever. I personally never received any money, nor anybody else who lived in that village of Zasavica to be compensated with money for the work that they performed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Roughly how long would you say that -- how many days or weeks were you required to go out on this plum-picking assignment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I spent on this assignment up to a day, when the International Red Cross entered Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you again tell us: Was it a matter of a few days that you spent on this assignment? Was it a week, or can you not remember roughly how many days you spent picking plums under armed guard?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately about a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned one of your other tasks as being looting. Can you tell us where you were taken to loot houses?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally worked on the looting of houses in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And these houses in Odzak, did you have any idea who they belonged to, what the ethnicity of the owner might be?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were houses belonging to people of ethnic -- of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And for what reason do you say that the houses belonged to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mother of my husband is from Odzak, and she is Muslim, so that I know that area very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you were taken to these houses, what were you instructed to do exactly to perform this looting?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't loot alone. The detainees from the school were looting together with me. Their task was to carry out the first stage of the looting, to take out the bigger objects, and this at the orders of the guards that were with us. After performing this duty, then I had the duty of bringing out lighter objects. It means clothing, carpets, paintings, pots and pans, all these valuables for which I was told that I should take out.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you were instructed, you and the other people with you, were instructed to remove all the contents of houses by the guards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told the place where we should put all these things nicely and leave them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you required to put these items onto trucks or simply take them to a designated area?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never loaded on any truck. I had to place these objects along the road, place them nicely, and that there would be easy access to these objects, easy and simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you have any information about where these household items would be taken after you had placed them in the assigned location?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was doing this, I knew exactly where these items would be taken, and I have also a reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Where would the items be taken, and what's the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will only state that what I know and what I've seen. At the time that I was in my apartment, as there was no electricity, I had to get a supply of firewood in order to be able to cook, and with the son of Luka Culumovic, I ensured a supply of firewood. And this firewood had to be placed in front of our entrance. An incident occurred, because at the same time, Vera Avdic, with a tractor, brought in - I know these were looted - now I know that these were looted items, and she brought them in front of this very same entrance. They took down from the tractor a stove, a cooking stove, a wood stove. I asked, "Where did you get it, Vera? I know that you don't have it." And she told me this was a reward for the participation of her husband in the 4th Detachment. And on that tractor, other items could be seen also. When I experienced this fact that I'm looting, I knew very well where these items would end, what kind of a reward they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So it was your personal understanding that the things you were removing from houses would later be distributed to Serbs and members of the Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You testified that you had to sweep or clean roads. Could you tell me where you had to clean roads?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the street in front of the mosque in Odzak, namely, the mosque had been destroyed, totally demolished, and the rocks, the debris which fell on the street, I had to sweep that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you the only one engaged in that task or were other detainees required to clear away the rubble of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the only one. There were more than one working on this. And we were either sent to this or that job, but we never were doing a job alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were clearing the rubble, were you also under the supervision of armed guards?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever we did was done under the supervision of armed guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you have any choice in what you did? Could you ever refuse to, for example, loot a particular house if you didn't want to?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no choice whatsoever. We had to perform that what was told, what we were told to do, even if it was a question of looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said that whilst you were picking plums, that you were receiving one meal a day. Was this also the case when you were performing other tasks, such as looting or clearing away rubble?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We always had this one mini meal a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if you want to take the break at half past. I was going to move into another area. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We still have a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Are you going onto another topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I was going to move on to another topic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Okay. I have a couple of questions. When you were in Zasavica and you were taken to Odzak for plum-picking or whatever the work assignment contained, you necessarily had to cross the River Bosna, and if my memory serves me well, the bridges over the River Bosna were blown up during a rather early stage of the war. How did you get over the river Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is indeed a very good question. All the bridges had been destroyed. We would come into Odzak into two ways. The first way, via a pontoon bridge which was located in Pisari, the border between Samac and Pisari, and we would continue via Dubica to Odzak. That was one of the routes. After that, this was being avoided due to incidents which I could mention later on. And then they would take us via an alternative route, via Modrica. That bridge was also demolished. But at this time, they made something like a pontoon between the two parts of the demolished bridge. You can well imagine what it looked like to cross this bridge with a truck, the part of the bridge, the part of the pontoon, and again the bridge. And that is how we came to Odzak, but with the risk of having to swim in that truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a further question. I've understood from your testimony that your little dog Pegi was very close to your heart. What happened to the dog during your stay in Zasavica or later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My dog, my Pegi lived in the same room in which Mirsada Ceribasic and I lived. So it was the two of us and Pegi who shared one bed. While I worked, the men who were detained there guarded Pegi. My dog Pegi was exchanged as a child, so I had a number of 29 plus 1. That's the number I was assigned. And this plus 1 signified a child that was with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll take our break and resume our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. You're continuing examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, in answer to His Honour's question before the break, you said that there were a number of incidents which happened en route to Odzak, and that's why later you took an alternative route. What was the nature of these incidents that would happen on the way to forced labour?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were incidents. During one of them, I had a fortune or misfortune to be present. The part of the road from Ruda to Dubica, or rather, to the pheasant farm, was held by men from Krajina. And then further on, from the pheasant farm to Odzak was the area held by local Serbs, meaning the 4th Detachment, and others who cooperated with them. It was a division of territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were you sometimes stopped by the men from Krajina who controlled part of the territory you had to pass through?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before this happened to me, I was told that men from Krajina had a practice of stopping the truck, and if they waved to the truck to stop, this truck had to stop. And then men from Krajina would take the women off the truck and then send them to work in Obudovac, where they had their headquarters, or they were sent to the pheasant farm. And I was told that these women had been raped. When I happened to be in the truck that was stopped by men from Krajina, I was so afraid of being perhaps raped that I jumped off the truck. I have to say, Your Honour, that I still suffer consequences from that jump. I have been treated, and my penultimate vertebra is damaged, so I have a spinal damage, but I managed to save myself from an even worse fate of potentially being raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said you jumped off that truck. Do I take it, then, that you hid from the men and later rejoined your group to continue with your forced labour assignment? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that took place on that pheasant farm, or rather, on that road. The corn was very high around the road, and there were many plum trees, so it was sort of a wildish area, area of wildish growth, so I managed to hide myself there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you manage to rejoin the truck after the men from Krajina had either left or allowed the truck to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the 4th Detachment had that area to themselves, so the area with plum trees was theirs, so to speak, and this is where my group was assigned to work. And I simply quietly joined them as if nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So I take it that you hid in this wild growth and then rejoined on foot your group who were picking plums. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. It wasn't a large area.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever speak to any of these women, any women who had been taken from the trucks by the men from Krajina, or did you just hear reports of it from third parties?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked with these women.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to any women who had been raped after she had been removed from the truck?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rape was something dishonourable and embarrassing to me, and out of respect for these women, I never asked them anything about it. Because, God forbid, that something like that should happen to me. It is certain that I would hesitate to talk about it. They told us that our job in Obudovac was to clean their rooms and to provide any kind of service to them that they needed. These women did not want to be very specific, but it was understood what that meant. And later on I found what had been happening there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say "later on," do you mean after you were finally exchanged and were free, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was then.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before the break you had said that you performed forced labour until you were visited by the International Committee of the Red Cross. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall the date or the approximate date on which the ICRC came to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it September or October?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October. I'm sorry. I apologise. It was October, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: About a month after you were arrested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And just to clarify an earlier answer that you gave in the record. Between the beginning of September and this date in the beginning of October, the sort of forced labour you carried out was everything you described, was it: Plum-picking, looting, cleaning of streets?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were work assignments that I had to do while I was driven in a truck to forced labour sites. So I did whatever was seasonal and what was required, whether it was potato harvesting or something else. So whatever was dictated by the season.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And this all took place between -- generally during the month of September 1992, was it?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you when the International Committee of the Red Cross came to Zasavica? Were you in the village itself or were you on a forced labour assignment?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, none of us went to work, probably because they knew that we would have a visit. This was the first visit at the international level. So the first visit to the camp in Zasavica. And because of that, I was in the house belonging to the Zecevic family.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did you learn that there was a representative of the International Committee for the Red Cross in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very ill at the time and I was in bed when Mr. Pandurevic came asking me to help myself and the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What was the cause of your illness that required you to remain in bed?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, due to spinal injury, I was quite bended. I had intense pain. When I jumped off the truck, I started bleeding, and after that I was unable to walk normally. It was terrible. You can imagine how it was, without proper hygiene, for a woman to live under those conditions. And since I had no contact with doctors, I had no idea what was going on with me, but I looked pitiful.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When Mr. Pandurevic came to ask you to help yourself and the others, what did he mean by that? What did he ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that in his house there was a team of the ICRC, that there were UNPROFOR forces there, police from Bosanski Samac, and a lady interpreter who, according to him, was not interpreting truthfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And how did he think that you would be able to help in this situation?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had heard from other prisoners that I spoke English. He said that he would, with the help of others, manage to get me into that room without any announcement, so I could listen to that interpretation, since the conversation was already ongoing, and that I should intervene if the interpretation was not truthful indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you go to Mr. Pandurevic's house, where the ICRC were?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I started off with him immediately. I came to that house. There were very many people there. All of the prisoners were there, in fact. They let me through because they had been expecting my arrival, and they let me go to the door of that room. There was a large table, large improvised table there, at which there was Simo Krunic sitting, who was the representative of the authorities in Bosanski Samac; a lady interpreter sat there, with a very distinct Serbian accent; and there were other people there as well whom I didn't know, but they apparently represented the ICRC and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you understand the conversation that was taking place in that room between the people you've described to us?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The lady interpreter said, in English, naturally, that in the village of Zasavica there are regular visits by a doctor and that the food supply is undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was this lady interpreter simply interpreting what the Serb authorities were saying to her? So in other words, it was originally told to her this was the situation and she translated that into English for the benefit of the ICRC delegates?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a total lie. One of the locals was speaking at that very moment and complaining about the lack of medical assistance, or any kind of assistance in terms of food. And I reacted impulsively at that moment. I simply stood in front of them at the table and I said, "This is a lie, a complete lie." The woman who is interpreting for you is twisting the situation." I introduced myself and said that I am asking for assistance. I said that I was very ill and that I couldn't stand up for a long time, that I was bleeding, that I had a spinal injury, that I was malnourished, that most of the people are in a similar condition. There were the elderly there, the children. I asked that a doctor be brought to us. I asked that, for a doctor to be brought while they were there, so we could be at least helped that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you convey this information as best you could in English or in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, at that time, spoke fairly good English, and I think that that was the last time in my life that I spoke English. I speak German today very well, but I can't speak English any more. I can understand it. Mr. Krunic was extremely angry upon learning that I corrected and interfered in their attempt to spread lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like a correction, because on page 37, line 16, the Prosecutor asked a question to which we have not heard an answer. The question was whether this lady was correctly interpreting what the Serb authorities were speaking or incorrectly. We did not hear the answer to that question. We did not hear the answer to the Prosecutor's question, who brought the doctor there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: If Mr. Lukic would wait, I am coming back to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, again I want to go back to what I asked you earlier. When you came into the room, were you able to tell whether or not it was the Serb authorities, the people who were running the place where you were staying in Zasavica, who were telling the Red Cross that there was regular supplies of food, et cetera, telling those lies about the conditions, or was this the initiative of the interpreter, or was it the authorities who were trying to tell the Red Cross that things were better than they were?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very good question. Mr. Krunic had the honour of addressing the interpreter, and the question that was put by the man who was complaining was verbatim as I related it here, or rather, the reply was that we had daily medical assistance and regular food supply. That means that Mr. Krunic was lying, and the interpreter translated that verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The man who was complaining, was he -- when you say "complaining," was he a person from the Red Cross or was this a detainee in Zasavica who was trying to explain the circumstances to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a detainee, somebody who was imprisoned just like I was. But after putting that question, he had nothing else to ask. All of us were afraid of being beaten, because beating was a regular occurrence in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, I need you to try to be very clear about what happened in this room, because it's confusing now on the record. You said Mr. Krunic addressed the interpreter. Is that correct? At one stage he was the person talking to the interpreter? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the one who talked to the interpreter. Mr. Krunic was the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mr. Krunic is, you said, I think, the representative of the Serb authorities from Bosanski Samac at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an official of the police in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So he was telling the interpreter that there was daily medical assistance and regular food supply; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the interpreter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy. When you say "Mr. Krunic was telling the interpreter," is that really what we're talking about, or is it a situation where we've got Mr. Krunic, then we've got the International Committee of the Red Cross and UNPROFOR representatives, and Mr. Krunic is talking -- or is Mr. Krunic talking to the reps of the ICRC and UNPROFOR, and the interpreter is simply interpreting? So he isn't talking to the interpreter; he's talking to them and she is interpreting, just like we have interpretation here? Could you clarify that that is the situation? And then secondly, for us to get clear, because I agree, there is some confusions on the transcript: Was the interpreter interpreting what she heard and verbatim saying it in English, or was she putting a gloss on it and not interpreting but rather elaborating in English, in some way that wasn't correct, interpretation of Mr. Krunic's words?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I hope I'm trying to go in that direction of answering all those queries.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When Mr. Krunic made his address or made his comments about daily medical assistance and regular food supply, was that then translated into English by this interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that Mr. Krunic was a dominant person in that room. He was the one who was the main speaker. And to give a specific reply to your question, let me say that Mr. Krunic said that we had food supplies and medical assistance, and this is exactly what the interpreter translated into English to the other gentlemen who were present there. That was the greatest lie, to say that in front of all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. But again, to clarify: Is it as Her Honour said, then, that Mr. Krunic was talking in B/C/S, in fact, addressing the delegates of the Red Cross, and that was being interpreted by the interpreter accompanying the Red Cross; he was putting into -- she was putting into English Mr. Krunic's words for the benefit of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So when you say -- again, you said verbatim. So she wasn't adding her own things. It was Mr. Krunic's words that she was translating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you've also mentioned someone who was complaining. Is this a separate person from Mr. Krunic?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complaints were made by the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And were the detainees trying to address the delegates of the Red Cross in the same way that Mr. Krunic had addressed them?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this type of intercourse wasn't possible. The complaints were made addressed to Mr. Krunic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So is it that the detainees addressed Mr. Krunic in B/C/S? That's it, is it?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But he was the sole one who conducted the conversation with the delegates of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And he would say that there was daily medication, regular food supply, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, we've been through all of that. Please, don't repeat the evidence all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I know what you're trying to say. He never addressed the complaints of the detainees to the Red Cross and the UNPROFOR representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear when Mrs. Kapetanovic said that they had spread their lies, that this was where this was emanating, how the whole conversation was conducted. But if it's clear from the record, I'm more than happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one small question for clarity's sake. Mrs. Kapetanovic, when the detainees, such as the gentleman you mention, were complaining to Mr. Krunic about the conditions in Zasavica, were those complaints made in B/C/S also translated by the interpreter into English so that the members of the International Committee of the Red Cross could hear about the need for medical attention for the detainees? So were those complaints also translated into English so that the ICRC members could understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
